meta.title: Who really said "There is always a well-known solution to every human problem—neat, plausible, and wrong"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Peter Drucker. H.L. Mencken wrote it in “The Divine Afflatus,” Prejudices: Second Series (1920). Drucker and Mark Twain are later misattributions.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is always a well-known solution to every human problem—neat, plausible, and wrong'?
meta.ogDescription: It’s H.L. Mencken, from Prejudices: Second Series (1920), not Peter Drucker — a documented misattribution traced by Quote Investigator.

answer.label: Not Peter Drucker — actually H.L. Mencken
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely Mencken’s, not Drucker’s. It appears in his essay “The Divine Afflatus” as published in Prejudices: Second Series (Alfred A. Knopf, 1920). Quote Investigator notes the sentence was added for the 1920 book — it is absent from the 1917 newspaper version of the essay — and that Peter Drucker and Mark Twain are later, unsupported attributions.

trail: Quote Investigator traces the exact wording to Mencken’s “The Divine Afflatus” in Prejudices: Second Series (1920) and finds no support for Twain or Drucker.
Wikiquote lists it in Mencken’s sourced quotations, citing “The Divine Afflatus” (1917 essay; collected in Prejudices: Second Series, 1920).

author.heading: About H.L. Mencken
author.bio: Henry Louis Mencken was a Baltimore newspaperman, critic, and satirist known as the “Sage of Baltimore.” His multi-volume Prejudices essays and his coverage of American culture made him one of the most influential and quotable American writers of the early twentieth century. His sharp aphorisms are frequently repackaged and, as here, misattributed to other famous names.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Drucker
misattribution.intro: This is one of Mencken’s most-borrowed lines. Its clever, contrarian ring makes it easy to reassign to other quotable authorities.

items.why: The management guru is a common modern credit, but Quote Investigator finds no instance of Drucker originating it — it predates his career and belongs to Mencken.
An older misattribution; QI reports “no substantive evidence that Mark Twain used this expression.”
The popular short form — e.g. “For every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple, and wrong” — swaps Mencken’s “well-known solution” and adjectives, per Wikiquote’s paraphrase note.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Mencken’s, first printed in Prejudices: Second Series (1920) — not Drucker’s and not Twain’s.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Mencken wrote the line in “The Divine Afflatus,” an essay skeptical of tidy theories of creativity and human behavior. His point is that satisfying explanations are cheap — and that their neatness is exactly what should make us distrust them.
The irony is that the aphorism itself became a “neat, plausible” line that people confidently misattribute — proving its own thesis about easy answers.
